title: The past: regular preterite
objectives: I can say what I did yesterday and last weekend using regular verbs in the past.
I can build the pretérito perfeito of any regular -ar, -er or -ir verb for every person, including a gente and eles, and say what each ending is made of.
I can explain why the eu form of verbs in -car, -çar and -gar changes its spelling (toquei, comecei, paguei) using the sound rules for c, g and ç.
I can explain why the preterite endings need no written accent while saí, saímos, há and atrás carry one.
I can ask and answer questions about past events and say what I did not do, with no word for did.
I can place events in time with ontem, anteontem, na semana passada, há dois dias, dois dias atrás and faz um mês que.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: on-tem. The o is nasal because the n ends its syllable, and the ending -em at the end of a word is the nasal diphthong [ẽj̃], the sound of bem and tem. The default for -em is the second to last syllable (ON-tem), so no accent is written. The t is a plain [t] because the vowel after it is the nasal e, not the sound [i].

example.pt: Ontem eu trabalhei muito.
example.en: Yesterday I worked a lot.

vocabulary.note: Built from ante-, 'before' (as in English 'antecedent'), and ontem. Spelling and sound: an-te-on-tem has four syllables. The e and o of -eon- are two strong vowels side by side, which never make a diphthong, so each has its own syllable. The stress stays on the same syllable as in ontem (an-te-ON-tem), which is the default for -em, so no accent is written.

example.pt: Anteontem choveu o dia inteiro.
example.en: The day before yesterday it rained all day.

vocabulary.note: Passada is the feminine form of the adjective passado, 'past'. An adjective follows its noun and agrees with it: a semana passada, o mês passado, o ano passado. After the preposition em the article contracts: na semana passada, no mês passado. In everyday speech the preposition and article are often dropped altogether: semana passada eu viajei.

example.pt: Na semana passada eu visitei a minha tia.
example.en: Last week I visited my aunt.
example.literal: In-the week past I visited the my aunt.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: mês is a stressed one-syllable word ending in -es, so it takes a circumflex (closed e). The plural meses has the default stress for -es, on the second to last syllable (ME-ses), so the accent disappears.

example.pt: No mês passado meu irmão mudou de emprego.
example.en: Last month my brother changed jobs.
example.literal: In-the month past my brother changed of job.

vocabulary.note: Há is the form of haver that means 'there is', the há of há vagas. Meaning 'ago', it comes before the period of time: há três meses, 'there-is three months', that is, three months lie between then and now. Spelling and sound: há is one stressed syllable ending in a, so it takes an acute accent, like já and nós. The accent also separates it from the unstressed preposition a. The h is silent.

example.pt: Comprei este celular há três meses.
example.en: I bought this phone three months ago.
example.literal: I-bought this cellphone there-is three months.

vocabulary.note: Atrás means 'behind' (Ele está atrás de mim, 'he is behind me'). In a time expression it follows the period of time, which is pictured as lying behind you: dois dias atrás. Very common in everyday speech, and it means the same as há dois dias. Spelling and sound: a-TRÁS ends in -as, whose default is the second to last syllable, but the stress is on the last, so an acute accent is written on the open a.

example.pt: Ele chegou dois dias atrás.
example.en: He arrived two days ago.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: fim ends in m, which nasalizes the i [ĩ], as in sim. In de, the d before a final unstressed e is said [dʒi].

example.pt: Eu descansei o fim de semana inteiro.
example.en: I rested the whole weekend.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: in fes-ta the s ends a syllable, so it is [s] in São Paulo and [ʃ] in the city of Rio de Janeiro; the final a is a weak 'uh'.

example.pt: A festa começou às nove da noite.
example.en: The party started at nine at night.
example.literal: The party started at-the nine of-the night.

vocabulary.note: Borrowed from English with its spelling, and said much as in English, [ʃow]. The pair sh is not a native Portuguese digraph; native words write [ʃ] with ch or x. The plural is shows. In Brazil it is the usual word for a concert.

example.pt: A gente assistiu a um show incrível.
example.en: We watched an incredible show.
example.literal: The-people attended to a show incredible.

vocabulary.note: Aniversário is the same word as English 'anniversary', the yearly return of any date, and used alone it means a birthday. Spelling and sound: a-ni-ver-SÁ-ri-o. The ending -rio counts as two syllables (ri-o) for the accent rules, so the stress is on the third to last syllable, and a word stressed there always carries an accent, as in sábado and música. Num in the example is the contraction of em and um, 'in a', built like na (em + a) and no (em + o).

example.pt: Ela comemorou o aniversário num restaurante.
example.en: She celebrated her birthday in a restaurant.
example.literal: She commemorated the anniversary in-a restaurant.

vocabulary.note: It comes from the same Latin source as English 'commemorate', but in everyday Portuguese it is the ordinary verb for celebrating a birthday or a victory. Regular -ar verb: comemorei, comemorou, comemoramos, comemoraram.

example.pt: Nós comemoramos o aniversário do Pedro no sábado.
example.en: We celebrated Pedro's birthday on Saturday.
example.literal: We commemorated the birthday of-the Pedro in-the Saturday.

vocabulary.note: Encontrar means 'to find', and when what you find is a person it means to meet or run into someone. Spelling and sound: en-con-TRAR has two nasal vowels (en [ẽ], con [õ]) because n ends each of those syllables, and the r after t is a tap.

example.pt: Encontrei um amigo antigo no mercado.
example.en: I ran into an old friend at the market.
example.literal: I-found a friend old in-the market.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: co-zi-NHAR. The pair nh is the single sound [ɲ], like 'ny' in canyon, and a z between vowels is [z]. The eu form is cozinhei (co-zi-NHEI).

example.pt: Meu pai cozinhou o almoço inteiro.
example.en: My father cooked the whole lunch.

vocabulary.note: In careful Brazilian Portuguese assistir takes the preposition a when it means to attend or watch something shown or performed: assistir a um filme, assistir ao show, assistir à aula (a + a = à). In everyday speech many Brazilians drop it. Spelling and sound: as-sis-TIR. A double ss between vowels is [s] (a single s there would be [z]), and in -tir the t comes before the sound [i], so it is said [tʃ].

example.pt: Assistimos a um filme ontem à noite.
example.en: We watched a movie last night.
example.literal: We-attended to a film yesterday at-the night.

vocabulary.note: Formally the thing answered takes the preposition a: responder à mensagem. In everyday speech Brazilians drop it and treat the thing answered as a direct object (the noun that receives the action with no preposition in between), so the a in responder a mensagem is just the article 'the'. The same goes for responder o cliente.

example.pt: Ela não respondeu a minha mensagem.
example.en: She did not answer my message.
example.literal: She not answered the my message.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: es-que-CER. The pair qu before e is [k] with a silent u, and the c before e is [s]. In the eu form of the preterite the spelling does not change (esqueci), because c before i is also [s]; compare tocar, where the c must change. Followed by a verb, esquecer takes de: esqueci de mandar, 'I-forgot of to-send'.

example.pt: Esqueci o celular em casa.
example.en: I forgot my phone at home.

vocabulary.note: An -ir verb: abri, abriu, abrimos, abriram. Spelling and sound: in abriu the ending -iu is one syllable (a-BRIU), a diphthong whose glide is u. The h of horas is silent.

example.pt: Abrimos a porta às oito horas.
example.en: We opened the door at eight o'clock.
example.literal: We-opened the door at-the eight hours.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: saí, saiu, saímos, saíram. Spelling and sound: sa-IR has two syllables, because the a and the stressed i do not form a diphthong. The accent on saí, saímos and saíram marks a stressed i that is alone in its syllable; saiu and sair need none because their i shares a syllable with u or r. The grammar note on stress works through this step by step.

example.pt: Saímos de casa muito cedo.
example.en: We left home very early.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: the eu form is paguei. The u is silent and keeps the g hard [g] before e, because a plain g before e would be [ʒ]. The other forms are regular: pagou, pagamos, pagaram.

example.pt: Paguei a conta do jantar.
example.en: I paid the dinner bill.

vocabulary.note: Tocar means 'to touch', and by extension to play an instrument (you touch the strings or keys) and to ring. Spelling and sound: the eu form is toquei. The qu keeps the hard [k] before e, because a plain c before e would be [s].

example.pt: Ele tocou violão na festa.
example.en: He played the guitar at the party.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: the eu form is comecei. The cedilla is never written before e or i, because a plain c there already means [s]; começou and começamos keep ç before o and a. Followed by a verb, começar takes a: comecei a estudar, 'I-started to study'.

example.pt: O show começou atrasado.
example.en: The show started late.

vocabulary.note: Spelling and sound: ch is [ʃ], like 'sh', and the eu form is cheguei, with a silent u that keeps the g hard. In everyday Brazilian speech chegar takes em for the place you arrive at (chegar em casa), where textbooks prescribe a.

example.pt: Cheguei em casa à meia-noite.
example.en: I got home at midnight.

grammar.title: The regular preterite: what it means and how it is built
grammar.explanation:
A tense is a set of verb forms that places an action in time (the lesson on how Portuguese works introduced the term). Portuguese has two main tenses for the simple past, and this course teaches them one at a time. This unit teaches the pretérito perfeito, called the preterite in English-language grammars. It presents a past action as finished and bounded: it happened, and it is over. Ontem eu trabalhei, 'yesterday I worked', reports one completed event. The word perfeito here does not mean flawless; it comes from a Latin word for 'completed'. The other past tense, the imperfect, comes in a later unit and describes background, habits and states that were going on. For now the working rule is this: a past event that is complete, with a definite moment, count or limit, takes the preterite.

English does the same job with the simple past (I worked, I danced), but the information sits in different places. An English regular past ends in -ed for every person (I worked, she worked, they worked), so the subject must always be said, and questions and negatives need a separate helper word, did (Did you work? I did not work). Portuguese changes the ending of the verb for each person, and that ending also carries the tense. The ending alone therefore tells you who acted, which is why the subject pronoun can usually be dropped, as the lesson on verbs explained.

To build the preterite, take the infinitive, remove -ar, -er or -ir to get the stem (fal-, com-, abr-), and add the ending for the person. The table shows each form as stem plus ending. Three patterns make the endings easy to remember. First, the vowel of the verb family (a, e or i) shows in the nós and eles forms (-amos, -emos, -imos; -aram, -eram, -iram) and in the você form of -er and -ir verbs (-eu, -iu); in the você form of -ar verbs the a has shifted to o (-ou). Second, the person markers are the same for all three families: a final -u for você, ele, ela and a gente, -mos for nós, and -ram for vocês, eles and elas. Third, the eu form is -ei for -ar verbs and -i for both -er and -ir verbs, so comi and abri end alike, and the -er and -ir families differ only in the family vowel in the other forms (comeu and abriu, comeram and abriram).

Brazil reduces the system, as it does in the present. Você, ele, ela and a gente share one form (a gente takes the third person singular because it literally means 'the people', a third-person noun), and vocês, eles and elas share one form. The second person singular tu has its own form (falaste), used in some regions and not needed here, and vós is archaic. The nós form (falamos, comemos, abrimos) is spelled exactly like the present nós form; European Portuguese writes falámos with an accent for the past, but Brazilian spelling does not. Context tells the tenses apart: a word like ontem makes the sentence past, and in speech a gente falou avoids the question altogether.

The third person plural shows the difference most clearly: falam (they speak) and falaram (they spoke) differ by one syllable, -ra-, which you can hear as well as read. The next note explains how the stress moves. One last point concerns choosing the tense. The preterite goes with moments and limits, such as ontem, às dez, na semana passada, duas vezes or por duas horas, because each of these closes the event. Markers of habit, such as todo dia or sempre, do not close an event; in the past they call for the imperfect, which a later unit teaches.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: where the stress falls in the preterite, and why no accent is written
grammar.explanation:
The lesson on stress gave Portuguese spelling a design: the last letters of a word predict which syllable is stressed, and a written accent appears only when a word breaks that prediction. Apply the design to the preterite endings and you can see why none of them needs an accent mark, although the stress sits in a different place from the present tense.

Start with the singular forms. The endings -ei, -ou, -eu and -iu are all diphthongs, a vowel followed by a quick glide written i or u (the lesson on sounds gave their values: ei [ej] as in 'day', eu [ew], iu [iw], and ou [ow], which in everyday speech often shrinks to a plain closed o). A word ending in a diphthong is stressed on its last syllable by default, so falei is fa-LEI, falou is fa-LOU, comeu is co-MEU and abriu is a-BRIU. The stress agrees with the default, so no accent is needed. The same endings explain why the stress moves compared with the present: falo is FA-lo, with the stress on the stem, but falei is fa-LEI, with the stress on the ending. The written difference is small and easy to miss. Falo (I speak) and falou (he or she spoke) differ by one letter, and that final u carries both the tense and the person. In the same way come (he eats) and comeu (he ate) differ only by the u, and the stress moves from CO-me to co-MEU.

The plural forms follow the defaults for -am and -os. Falaram, comeram and abriram end in -am, a nasal ending that belongs to the group (a, e, o, am, em, ens) stressed on the second to last syllable: fa-LA-ram, co-ME-ram, a-BRI-ram. Compare the present falam, FA-lam, which has one syllable fewer. So in speech you hear the past plural as an extra syllable with a later stress, and in writing as the extra letters -ra-. The nós forms (falamos, comemos, abrimos) end in -os and are stressed on the second to last syllable, fa-LA-mos, co-ME-mos, a-BRI-mos, exactly as in the present.

The one verb in this unit that does carry accents is sair, and it carries them for a different reason, the hiatus rule from the lesson on stress. A hiatus is two vowels side by side that belong to different syllables. In sair the a and the i are separate syllables (sa-IR), and the i is the stressed one. The rule says that a stressed i or u in the second place of a hiatus is written with an acute accent when it is alone in its syllable, or followed only by s, because otherwise the reader would take the pair for a diphthong. So saí is sa-Í, saímos is sa-Í-mos and saíram is sa-Í-ram, each with an accented i alone in its syllable. In saiu the i is followed by u in the same syllable (sa-IU), and in sair it is followed by r in the same syllable, so the i is not alone and no accent is written. The accent here does not mark the stress, since the default would already put the stress in the right place; it only says that the i is not a glide. The table sets each form beside what its ending predicts.

no, the i shares its syllable with u
yes, í alone in its syllable (hiatus)

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: why -car, -çar and -gar verbs change in the eu form
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is a code for sounds, and the lesson on sounds gave the rules of the code. The verbs in this note do not break the preterite pattern. They apply the spelling code to it: the stem keeps its sound, so the letters that write that sound must change when the letter after it changes.

Recall the rules. The letter c is [k] before a, o and u and [s] before e and i, so to write [k] before e or i you write qu, where the u is silent. The letter g is [g] before a, o and u and [ʒ], the s of 'measure', before e and i, so to write [g] before e or i you write gu, where the u is silent. The letter ç, c with a cedilla, writes [s] before a, o and u, and it is never written before e or i, where a plain c already means [s].

Now look at the preterite endings of -ar verbs, the only family where the stem meets a hard c or g in the eu form. Only one of them begins with e: the eu ending -ei. The others begin with o or a (-ou, -amos, -aram). Take tocar, whose stem toc- ends in the sound [k]. Before the o of tocou and the a of tocamos the c is still [k], so nothing changes. Before the e of -ei a plain c would be [s], and tocei would be said to-SEI. To keep [k] the spelling becomes toquei. The same logic gives pagar: pagou, pagamos, but paguei, because pagei would be said pa-JEI. With ç the problem runs the other way: começar has the stem começ-, ending in [s]. Começou and começamos keep the ç before o and a, but ç is never written before e, so the eu form is comecei, with the plain c that already means [s] there. In every form the sound of the stem is the same; only the letters differ.

You can check any such verb by sound alone: say the last consonant of the stem in the infinitive, say it again in the eu form, and make sure it is the same. The u in toquei and paguei is silent (it only protects the hard sound, as in que and gue); do not pronounce it like the u in quando. In cheguei, ch is [ʃ] and gu is [g].

Two things do not change. First, -er and -ir verbs have the eu ending -i, and c and g are already soft before i, exactly as before the e of the infinitive, so esquecer gives esqueci with no change: the c is [s] in both. Second, the present tense eu form ends in -o, so -car and -gar verbs have no problem there (toco, pago, começo). The mirror problem exists for -cer and -ger verbs in the present, where the o needs a ç to keep the sound [s]: esquecer gives esqueço. The rule behind all of these is the same: whenever an ending that begins with e or i follows a hard c or g, or an ending that begins with a, o or u follows a soft one, the spelling adjusts to keep the sound.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the other written forms in this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every written form in this unit can be explained with the same small toolkit from the first lessons. This note walks through the words most likely to look strange, and the table gives each one a rule. The method is the one from the lesson on stress: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable, read the default from the ending, and write an accent only where the word breaks the default.

Accents that mark a stress the ending does not predict. Atrás (a-TRÁS), até (a-TÉ), ninguém (nin-GUÉM) and parabéns (pa-ra-BÉNS) are stressed on the last syllable, although the endings -as, -e, -em and -ens default to the second to last, so each carries an accent. Sábado, música, aniversário and escritório are stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so they always carry an accent; the endings -rio and -ria count as two syllables (ri-o), which is why aniversário and escritório belong to this group. Incrível is stressed on the second to last syllable while the ending -l defaults to the last, so it needs an accent too. In every case the quality of the vowel chooses the mark: acute for an open a, e or o, circumflex for a closed e or o.

One-syllable words and the three a's. A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o takes an accent: há, já, né, só and, with s, mês and três. Né is the speech form of não é, 'not is', added to the end of a statement to ask for agreement, like 'right?' or 'isn't it?'. Three different words are spelled with a: há, with the acute, is the verb form meaning 'there is'; a, with no mark, is the unstressed preposition 'to' or 'at'; and à, with the grave, is that preposition fused with the article a (the lesson on accent marks called this crase). Compare há três meses, 'there-is three months' (ago), a que horas, 'at what hours', where a is only the preposition, and à noite, 'at-the night', where the preposition and the article have merged. The fusion with the plural article gives às: às nove, 'at-the nine' (the hour is feminine, as in as nove horas). A quick test: if a masculine word in the same place would take ao, the feminine word takes à.

Nasal vowels and digraphs. In ontem, também, ninguém and mensagem the final -em is the nasal diphthong [ẽj̃]; in fim and ainda the i is nasal because an m or n ends its syllable; ão in violão and feijão is the nasal diphthong [ɐ̃w̃], stressed on the last syllable by default; and the tilde in manhã marks a nasal vowel and, when no other accent is present, the stress. The pairs nh, lh and ch are single sounds: cozinhei (co-zi-NHEI), trabalhei (tra-ba-LHEI), chegar. The u of qu and gu is silent before e and i: esqueci, que, paguei. A double ss between vowels is [s] (assistir). The letter h is silent (há, hoje, horas). An l that ends a syllable is said [w], so almoçou is aw-mo-SOU, with the ç as [s] before o. The letters t and d before the sound [i] become [tʃ] and [dʒ]: noite, tarde, de. In descansar the s ends the syllable and the c before a is [k], so the sequence is [sk], unlike the sc of descer.

Borrowed words keep their spelling. Show is said much as in English, [ʃow], and shopping begins with the same sh; its final -ing is a nasal i, with no g sound. E-mail is written with a hyphen, like a compound word, and said ee-MAY-oo. Táxi has an x that is [ks], and it is stressed on the first syllable where the ending -i would predict the last, so it takes an accent. Arroz is written with rr between vowels, the strong [h].

grammar.title: Past time markers and the three ways to say ago
grammar.explanation:
A time marker tells the listener when something happened, and in the preterite it also supplies the moment or limit that closes the event. Portuguese time markers are short and follow patterns, so it is worth seeing the patterns rather than memorizing a list.

Three words anchor the past: ontem (yesterday), anteontem (ante-, 'before', plus ontem, so 'before-yesterday') and hoje (today) when the part of today you mean is already over, as in hoje de manhã. They combine with parts of the day: ontem de manhã (yesterday morning, literally 'of morning'), ontem à tarde and ontem à noite. Notice that de manhã uses de, while à tarde and à noite use the fused à from the previous note. Longer periods use the adjective passado, 'past', which follows its noun and agrees with it: a semana passada (feminine), o mês passado and o ano passado (masculine). After a preposition the article contracts, as the lesson on contractions explained: na semana passada, no mês passado, no ano passado. In speech the preposition and article are often dropped completely: semana passada eu viajei. A bounded duration closes an event as well and takes the preterite: conversamos por horas, 'we-talked for hours'; a noite toda, 'the night whole'; o dia inteiro, 'the day whole'. Toda, todo and inteiro agree with the noun in gender; in these phrases they follow it (a noite toda, o dia inteiro), and toda a noite, with toda first, means the same.

English has one word for 'ago', placed after the time. The word is a relic of an old verb meaning 'gone by', so 'two days ago' is roughly 'two days gone'. Portuguese has three patterns, each picturing the same fact differently. Há dois dias is word for word 'there-is two days': há is the haver of há vagas, and the phrase says that two days lie between then and now. The time comes after há. Dois dias atrás is 'two days behind': the period is pictured as lying behind you, and it comes before atrás. This is the pattern you will hear most in speech. Faz dois dias que, followed by a clause (a group of words with its own verb), is word for word 'makes two days that', and it means 'it has been two days since': Faz um mês que eu comecei o curso. The verb after que is in the preterite when the event itself is finished (comecei), and in the present when the situation is still going on: Faz dois anos que eu moro aqui means 'I have lived here for two years', where English needs a present perfect and Portuguese uses the present.

Do not confuse há with a. Há plus a period looks backwards (há dois dias, two days ago), whereas the preposition a in daqui a dois dias looks forwards: 'from-here at two days', that is, in two days. Daqui is the contraction of de and aqui, 'from here'. Finally, the position of a marker is free and the verb order does not change: Ontem eu comprei pão and Eu comprei pão ontem are both normal. When the marker comes first, the subject pronoun is often dropped: Ontem comprei pão.

grammar.title: Questions and negation in the past, with no word for did
grammar.explanation:
English splits the past tense in two when it asks or denies. The helper did carries the tense, and the main verb goes back to its base form: You paid, but Did you pay? and You did not pay. Portuguese has no helper of this kind. The tense lives in the ending of the verb, so the verb keeps its full preterite form in a question and in a negative, and nothing else in the sentence has to change.

A yes or no question is the statement with a rising voice: Você pagou a conta? An information question puts the question word first and then the sentence in its normal order: Quando você chegou? Onde vocês almoçaram? Quanto você pagou? Com quem você conversou? A que horas você saiu? A preposition belongs to the question word and stays in front of it, where English often leaves it at the end of the sentence: com quem is 'with whom', and the English question is 'who did you talk to?'. A que horas is 'at what hours', 'at what time'. A tag such as né at the end of a statement asks for confirmation: Vocês chegaram tarde, né?

To deny, place não directly before the verb: Eu não comprei pão. The words nada (nothing, anything), ninguém (nobody, anybody) and nunca (never) are negative words. Portuguese not only allows a double negative; it requires one in one position. When the negative word comes after the verb, não must also stand before the verb: Eu não encontrei ninguém, word for word 'I not found nobody'. When the negative word comes before the verb, não is dropped: Ninguém respondeu, Nunca esqueci. English treats two negatives as a mistake, but in Portuguese the rule is simply one of two shapes: a negative word before the verb, or não before the verb plus a negative word after it. Ainda não means 'not yet'. It uses the simple preterite where English uses 'have not ... yet': Ainda não abri o e-mail, word for word 'still not I-opened the email'. It points to an event that has not happened up to now.

The short answer repeats the verb, with its person changed to match the speaker: Você pagou a conta? Paguei. Não paguei. The yes or no is carried by the verb itself, where English carries it with 'I did'. Sim, paguei is also correct and sounds a little more emphatic.

Finally, many verbs require a particular preposition before what follows, and the preposition cannot be guessed from English. Gostar de: Você gostou do show? (gostou de + o show, with the contraction from the lesson on contractions). Esquecer de plus a verb: Esqueci de mandar. Começar a plus a verb: Comecei a estudar. Assistir a: Assistimos a um filme. Learn each verb together with its preposition, as one unit.

culture.title: Talking about the weekend
culture.text:
On Monday morning, almost every Brazilian office starts with the same question: E aí, como foi o fim de semana? The foi is a form of ser that a later unit teaches; for now it is enough to know that the question means 'how was the weekend?'. Colleagues trade stories about a churrasco, a barbecue at a friend's house, a balada, a night out at a club or party, or a rolê, a casual outing with no fixed plan. Friday evening is greeted with sextou, a joke built on sexta, Friday. Its ending -ou is the third person singular preterite ending you have just learned, so sextou behaves like a made-up verb form, roughly 'it has Fridayed', and it announces that the weekend has started.

Social life revolves around food, music and family. Birthdays are a big event: it is normal to invite relatives, neighbours and old friends, to sing parabéns pra você and to cut the bolo with a lot of noise. Guests often arrive later than the time printed on the invitation, and a party that starts at nine can easily go on until the early morning. That is why so many stories about the weekend begin with A gente chegou tarde, mas valeu a pena, word for word 'the-people arrived late, but was-worth the pain', which means 'we arrived late, but it was worth it'. Valer a pena is a fixed expression, and valeu is its preterite form.

Another habit worth knowing is the use of a gente in storytelling. In everyday conversation people often prefer a gente comeu and a gente dançou to nós comemos and nós dançamos. It sounds warmer, and it avoids the confusion between the nós form of the preterite and the nós form of the present, which are spelled exactly alike.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with its word-for-word meaning
Which ending marks the eu form of a regular -ar verb in the preterite?
exercises.explanation: Eu takes -ei for -ar verbs (falei) and -i for -er and -ir verbs (comi, abri). The ending -ou is for você, ele, ela and a gente.

exercises.explanation: Acordar is an -ar verb, so its stem acord- takes the eu ending -ei.

exercises.prompt: Qual é a forma certa? A gente ___ bolo ontem.
exercises.explanation: A gente literally means 'the people', a third person singular noun, so it takes the same verb form as ele and ela: comeu.

exercises.prompt: Why is there no written accent on falou although the stress is on the last syllable?
choices: The ending -ou is a diphthong, and a word ending in a diphthong is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the stress agrees with the default
Accents are never written on verbs
Because falou is in the present tense
exercises.explanation: An accent is written only when a word breaks the default for its ending. Falou does not, so it needs none.

exercises.explanation: Both endings -em and -am default to the second to last syllable. Comeram has one more syllable than comem, so the stressed e moves one place to the right.

Because começar is an irregular verb
Because the eu ending after ç is -ai
exercises.explanation: The sound stays [s]. Começou and começamos keep the ç because it stands before o and a.
A plain g before e would be [ʒ], so pagar adds a silent u in the eu form: paguei.

exercises.prompt_pt: No sábado eu ___ com a minha tia.

exercises.explanation: The stem almoç- ends in [s]. The ç is never written before e, so the eu form has a plain c: almocei. Almoçou and almoçamos keep the ç before o and a.

exercises.prompt: Which of these verbs needs a spelling change in the eu form of the preterite?

exercises.prompt: Why does mês carry an accent while its plural meses does not?

In meses the stress is on the second to last syllable, which is the default for the ending es, so no accent is needed

Falaram has one more syllable than the present falam, and eles is plural.
Sair has an i that is stressed and alone in its syllable, sa-Í, so it takes an accent.

exercises.prompt: Why does saímos have an accent on the í while saiu has none?

Because the accent marks an open vowel
exercises.explanation: The accent prevents the reader from taking the pair for a diphthong.
Há, the verb form meaning 'there is', followed by a period of time means 'ago'. The accent on há is the one-syllable rule for a stressed word ending in a.
